newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Senate approves key land reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Senate approves key land reform bill.

text.p: Brazil's Senate approved on Tuesday a bill aimed at speeding up the country's lagging land reform programme and considered crucial to the government's efforts to reduce violent conflict.

Left-wing deputies cheered when the upper house voted unanimously in favour of the bill. It establishes maximum time periods for stages of the reform process, which takes unused farmland from big landowners and gives it to landless families.
The bill, which will become law once signed by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, also reduces the opportunity for landowners to delay the reform procedure by appealing in court.
"Brazil can no longer tolerate the existence of vast farms which are run on a semi-feudal basis and often use slave labour," said Sen. Roberto Freire of the Popular Social Party.
Delays in executing land reform can often take years to resolve and are commonly a factor in land disputes that turn violent.
In April, police killed 19 landless peasants in a clash over rights to a huge Amazonian estate earmarked for redistribution. Its transfer was the subject of a lengthy court battle.

Brazil has one of the world's most unequal land distribution ratios with an estimated 44 percent of farmland in the hands of just one percent of landowners, according to the Catholic Church's Pastoral Land Commission.

The bill's approval was welcomed by Brazil's Landless Movement (MST), which claims nearly five million families need land. It encourages them to invade unused farms to pressure the government into speeding up reform.
"Of course this won't solve the problem of agrarian reform on its own, but it is a step in the right direction," said Gilberto Portes, a member of the MST's national directorate.

Approval of the bill came just one day before a joint session of Congress was due to vote on a presidential decree creating a stiff new tax on unused farmland, equivalent to 20 percent of the property's value.
The decree is considered the government's boldest step so far towards addressing Brazil's land distribution problems.
